entry: Branch of engineering concerned with the development of [[Aircraft|aircraft]] and [[Spacecraft|spacecraft]]. It has two major and overlapping branches, aeronautical engineering and astronautical engineering, while avionics engineering deals with the electronics side of the field. “Aeronautical engineering” was the original term, and “aerospace engineering” came into use as flight extended into outer space. The discipline draws on [[Aerodynamics|aerodynamics]], propulsion, avionics, [[Materials science|materials science]], structural analysis and manufacturing. In December 1903 the [[Wright brothers]] made the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft, lasting 12 seconds. The first definition of aerospace engineering appeared in February 1958, treating Earth’s atmosphere and outer space as a single realm. The Soviet launch of [[Sputnik 1|Sputnik]] on October 4, 1957 prompted U.S. aerospace engineers to launch the first American satellite.

Company engaged in designing, building, testing, selling and maintaining [[Aircraft|aircraft]], aircraft parts, [[Missile|missiles]], [[Rocket|rockets]] or [[Spacecraft|spacecraft]]. Aerospace is a high-technology industry. The aircraft industry builds aircraft and manufactures parts for their maintenance, serving both civil and military aviation, and most production is done under type certificates and Defense Standards issued by a government body. The term has been largely subsumed by “aerospace industry.” Aircraft production was worth US$180.3 billion in 2015, of which 61% was airliners and 12% military aircraft. The global aerospace industry was worth $838.5 billion in 2017, and the [[United States]] accounted for $408.4 billion, or 49% of the whole. The Department of Defense and [[NASA]] are the two biggest consumers of aerospace technology and products in the United States.

Ancient Greek tragedian, often described as the father of [[Tragedy|tragedy]]. Born in Eleusis, near [[Athens]], he fought against the Persians at [[Battle of Marathon|Marathon]] and later at Salamis and Plataea. According to [[Aristotle]], he expanded the number of characters on stage and allowed conflict among them, where earlier characters had interacted only with the chorus. He wrote an estimated 70 to 90 plays, of which seven survive in complete form, including the *Oresteia*, the only extant ancient trilogy. He was likely the first dramatist to present plays as a trilogy. *The Persians*, his oldest surviving play, was performed in 472 BC and won first prize at the Dionysia; it is one of very few classical Greek tragedies concerned with contemporary events. His epitaph commemorates his part in the Greek victory at Marathon and makes no mention of his success as a playwright.

Collection of fables credited to Aesop, a slave and storyteller of [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]]. The fables were part of [[Oral tradition|oral tradition]] and were not collected until about three centuries after Aesop’s death. Other stories, jokes and proverbs were later ascribed to him, and modern scholars do not regard him as the originator of all the fables attributed to him. [[Herodotus]] mentioned “Aesop the fable writer” in passing, and [[Plato]] reports that [[Socrates]] turned some of Aesop’s fables into verse. Manuscripts in Latin and Greek transmitted the fables, and collections were among the earliest books printed in many languages. Initially addressed to adults and covering religious, social and political themes, they were used to educate children from the [[Renaissance]] onward. Their characters are often talking animals and plants, and they typically close with a moral.

Kinship tie formed by marriage, linking each spouse to the blood relatives of the other. It is distinct from [[Consanguinity|consanguinity]], or blood kinship, and is essentially a social or moral construct, though it can carry legal consequences. Affinity sometimes ends with the death of a spouse or with divorce, and it may also include kinship by adoption or a step relationship. In law, affinity relatives are called affines; in common usage they are known as in-laws. The degree of affinity equals the consanguineal degree of the joined couple, so a husband’s relation to his sister-in-law is of the second degree. Affinity may be relevant to prohibitions on [[Incest|incestuous]] relations and marriages, which vary by jurisdiction. In [[South Africa]], sexual relations are prohibited within the first degree of affinity, and in [[Hawaii]] sexual penetration and marriage within close degrees of affinity are punishable by up to five years.

Series of events keeping Afghanistan in near-continuous armed conflict since the 1970s. A largely non-violent 1973 coup deposed the Afghan monarch Mohammad Zahir Shah, ending his 40-year-long reign. All-out fighting erupted after the Saur Revolution of 1978, and in 1979 the [[Soviet Union]] intervened, starting the [[Soviet–Afghan War]], in which mujahideen fighters received support from Pakistan, the United States and Saudi Arabia. The Soviets withdrew in 1989. After the Peshawar Accord failed in 1992, mujahideen factions fought a civil war, and by 1996 the [[Taliban]] controlled [[Kabul]] and approximately 90% of the country. Following the [[September 11 attacks]] of 2001, the Taliban refused to extradite [[Osama bin Laden]], and an American-led invasion toppled their regime. The resulting 20-year-long war saw [[NATO]] fight the Taliban insurgency. Bin Laden was killed in Abbottabad in 2011. After the 2020–2021 American withdrawal, the Taliban offensive of 2021 re-established the Islamic Emirate.

Landlocked country at the crossroads of Central and South Asia. Its capital and largest city is [[Kabul]], and it borders [[Pakistan]], [[Iran]], Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and China. It covers 652,864 sq km (252,072 sq mi), predominantly mountainous, with plains in the north and southwest separated by the [[Hindu Kush]]. The modern state began with the Durrani Empire of the 18th century under [[Ahmad Shah Durrani]]. Afghanistan was a buffer state in the [[Great Game]], and after the Third Anglo-Afghan War of 1919 it became independent as the Kingdom of Afghanistan in 1926. Since the late 1970s its history has been dominated by coups, invasions, insurgencies and civil wars. The [[Taliban]] returned to power in 2021 after capturing Kabul; their government is widely unrecognized internationally, owing to reported human rights violations, particularly regarding women. The country is rich in lithium, iron, zinc and copper, and it is the world’s third-largest producer of both saffron and cashmere, yet it remains among the world’s least developed countries.

First king of Portugal (r. 1139–1185). Son of Theresa of León and Henry of Burgundy, rulers of the County of Portugal, he is known as “the Conqueror” and “the Founder.” He defeated his mother at the Battle of São Mamede in 1128 and became sole count. In 1139 he renounced the suzerainty of León, won a decisive victory at the Battle of Ourique and established the independent Kingdom of Portugal. He doubled the kingdom’s area through the [[Reconquista]], seizing Santarém and [[Lisbon]] from the Moors in 1147 with help from crusaders bound for the Holy Land during the Second Crusade. He secured Portugal’s independence after a victory over León at Valdevez and received papal approval through the bull *Manifestis Probatum*. He was succeeded by his son Sancho I.

Portuguese general, admiral and conquistador; viceroy of Portuguese India (1509–1515). He also held the title 1st Duke of Goa. He pursued the Portuguese aims of combating Islam, spreading Christianity and securing the spice trade by building a Portuguese Asian empire. He conquered [[Goa]] in 1510 and captured Malacca in 1511, and he was the first European of the Renaissance to raid the [[Persian Gulf]]. He also led the first voyage by a European fleet into the [[Red Sea]], and his strategy aimed to close the Indian Ocean’s naval passages, making it a Portuguese *mare clausum*. As governor he oversaw diplomatic contacts with the [[Ayutthaya Kingdom]], Pegu in Myanmar, Timor and the Moluccas, and [[Ethiopia]], and he established ties with Persia under the [[Safavid dynasty]]. He received epithets such as “the Terrible” and “the Caesar of the East.”

Variety of [[American English|American English]] natively spoken by most working-class and middle-class Black Americans. Sometimes called Ebonics, a controversial name, it shares much of its grammar and phonology with the regional dialects of the [[Southern United States]], reflecting the historical enslavement of African Americans primarily in that region. Most linguists trace it to non-standard English dialects of settlers in the Southern Colonies and later the South; a minority argue that it originated as a [[Creole language|creole]] before converging with English.

American racial and ethnic group with ancestry from “any of the Black racial groups of Africa.” As of July 1, 2024, the overall Black population of the United States was estimated at 42,951,595, approximately 12.63% of the total. Most descend from people enslaved in the United States, brought through the [[Atlantic slave trade]] from the 16th century. Their contribution to popular music is so profound that most American popular music, including [[Blues|blues]], [[Jazz|jazz]] and [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], has origins partly or entirely in the African-American community.

Series of rift lakes in and around the East African Rift. It includes [[Lake Victoria]], the second-largest freshwater lake in the world by area; [[Lake Tanganyika]], the second-largest by volume and depth; [[Lake Malawi]], the fourth-largest by volume; and [[Lake Turkana]], the world’s largest permanent desert lake and largest alkaline lake. Together they hold 31,000 km³ (7,400 mi³) of water, about 25% of the planet’s unfrozen surface fresh water, and they are home to 10% of the world’s fish species. Ten riparian countries include [[Kenya]], [[Tanzania]] and [[Uganda]]. [[Swahili]] is the most commonly spoken language in the region, and it is a national or official language of five of its nations. The region suffered civil war and conflict c. 1980–2020.

South African political party formed as a liberation movement opposed to [[Apartheid|apartheid]]. Founded on January 8, 1912, in [[Bloemfontein]] as the South African Native National Congress, it was banned from April 1960 to February 1990, and from exile it waged armed struggle through uMkhonto weSizwe. It has governed South Africa since 1994, when [[Nelson Mandela]] was elected president. In the 2024 general election it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time, though it remained the largest party with just over 40% of the vote.

Group of ethnicities native to [[Central Africa]], mostly in the Congo Basin, traditionally living as [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]]. Named for their short stature, they are divided into western Bambenga or Mbenga, eastern Bambuti or Mbuti, and central and southern Batwa or Twa groups. Most now forage partially and trade with neighboring farmers for cultivated foods. About 900,000 people were estimated to live in the central African forests in 2016, about 60% of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The term “Pygmy” dates to the early 19th century and is considered pejorative, with many people preferring the names of their own groups, such as Bayaka, Mbuti and Twa. They have been widely affected by enslavement at the hands of neighboring Bantu, Ubangian and Central Sudanic groups.

Continental union of 55 member states on the African continent. The AU was launched on July 9, 2002, in [[Durban]], South Africa, replacing the Organization of African Unity, which had been established on May 25, 1963, in [[Addis Ababa]] by 32 signatory governments. Its secretariat, the African Union Commission, is based in Addis Ababa. Decisions are made by the Assembly of the African Union, a semi-annual meeting of heads of state and government. Its objectives include defending member states’ sovereignty and territorial integrity and promoting democratic principles and human rights. The Pan-African Parliament consists of 265 members elected by the national legislatures. The AU is a member of the [[G20]].

Visual art, including sculpture, painting, metalwork and pottery, from the peoples of the African continent. It prioritizes conceptual and symbolic representation over realism, aiming to visualize the subject’s spiritual essence, and it was often made for practical, spiritual or didactic purposes. [[Mask|Masks]] and human figures are important, and sculpture is most common among settled cultivators in the areas drained by the Niger and Congo rivers. West African cultures developed bronze casting, including the Benin Bronzes, which include highly naturalistic royal heads from around Benin City made from the 12th–14th centuries. Akan gold weights, produced from 1400 to 1900, sometimes represent proverbs. Ethiopian art, shaped by its long-standing Christian tradition, differs from most African art. Appreciation of African sculpture is credited with the concept of “African art” as seen by European and American artists.

Large bovine (*Syncerus caffer*) native to sub-Saharan Africa, the only extant species of its genus. First described in 1779 by Anders Sparrman, it has four recognized subspecies, including the Cape buffalo and the forest buffalo. It is heavily built, with large horns and a bony “boss” across the forehead of males. It lives in habitats ranging from woodlands and [[Savanna|savannas]] to forests, grasslands and wetlands, and it grazes in herds from a few individuals to over a thousand. Its lifespan is about 12 years in the wild. Since the 19th century its range has greatly reduced through poaching, climate change, agriculture and disease. As of 2019 it is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List, with an estimated 398,000 to 401,000 mature individuals. A Big Five game animal, it is legally hunted as a trophy in 16 out of 37 range countries.

Elephant species native to sub-Saharan Africa and the largest living terrestrial animal. Fully grown bulls reach an average shoulder height of 3.04–3.36 m and a body mass of 5.2–6.9 t. Cows live in herds with their offspring, while adult bulls usually live alone or in small groups. The average adult consumes about 150 kg of vegetation a day, and gestation lasts around 22 months, the longest of any mammal. Listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2021, it is threatened foremost by habitat destruction and, in parts of its range, by poaching for meat and [[Ivory|ivory]].

Literature from Africa, either oral (“orature”) or written in African and Afro-Asiatic languages. Pre-colonial examples date to at least the fourth century AD, including the 14th-century *Kebra Negast* (“Book of Kings”) and the *Garima Gospels*, written in Ge’ez around AD 500. Colonial-era writing often took the form of slave narratives written in English or French for Western audiences. [[Chinua Achebe]]’s *Things Fall Apart*, published in 1958, was among the first African works to receive worldwide critical acclaim. [[Wole Soyinka]] won the 1986 [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature, the first awarded to an African. Post-colonial writing is increasingly diverse, and female writers are far better represented than before independence. The internet has brought digital publishing platforms such as OkadaBooks.

Wild [[Canidae|canine]] native to sub-Saharan Africa, the only extant member of the genus *Lycaon*. Also called painted dog and Cape hunting dog, it is the largest wild canine in Africa. An estimated 6,600 adults, including 1,400 mature individuals, live in 39 subpopulations, and it has been listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 1990. It hunts [[Ungulate|ungulates]] mostly at dawn and dusk, exhausting prey through stamina and cooperative hunting, and its main competitors are [[Lion|lions]] and spotted hyenas.

Hybrid of the [[Western honey bee|western honey bee]], bred from the African honey bee and European honey bee subspecies. Also called the “killer bee,” it is much more defensive than other honey bees, reacts faster to disturbances and chases people up to 400 m (1,300 ft). It has killed some 1,000 humans, and its victims receive 10 times more stings than those stung by European honey bees. [[Brazil]] introduced African honey bees in 1956 to increase honey production. In 1957, 26 swarms with their queens escaped from an experimental apiary and crossbred with European colonies. The hybrid spread through South America and reached North America in 1985, and hives were found in southern [[Texas]] in 1990.

West Germanic language spoken mainly in [[South Africa]] and Namibia. It emerged in the late 19th century from Dutch dialects spoken by settlers since the 17th century, mixed with Dutch-based [[Creole language|creole]] languages spoken by the Khoisan, Nguni and Coloured peoples. An estimated 90 to 95% of its vocabulary is of Dutch origin. Its name derives from the Dutch word *Afrikaansch*, meaning “African.” In 2022 it was spoken by 10.6% of the South African population (6.3 million people), the third most spoken home language in the country.

Language family of about 400 languages spoken mainly in West Asia, North Africa and the Horn of Africa. Over 600 million people are native speakers, making it the fourth-largest family after Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan and Niger–Congo. Most linguists divide it into six branches: [[Berber languages|Berber]], Chadic, Cushitic, Egyptian, Omotic and [[Semitic languages|Semitic]]. [[Arabic]] is by far the most widely spoken, with an estimated 300 to 411 million native speakers. Extinct ancient members include Egyptian and the Semitic languages Akkadian and Biblical Hebrew. Scholars disagree on the homeland of Proto-Afroasiatic, the common ancestor; most place it in eastern North Africa or northern East Africa, while a significant minority argue for the Levant. Writing in its Semitic and Egyptian branches dates to the fourth millennium BC.

Mythical king of Mycenae and commander of the Achaean forces in the [[Trojan War]]. He was the son, or grandson, of King Atreus, the brother of Menelaus and the husband of Clytemnestra. In [[Homer]]’s *Iliad* he quarrels with [[Achilles]] over the captive Briseis. On his return from Troy he was killed by Clytemnestra, or, in an older version, by her lover Aegisthus. His death is the subject of [[Aeschylus]]’s tragedy *Agamemnon*, the first play of the *Oresteia* trilogy.

Genus of [[Mushroom|mushroom]]-forming fungi containing both edible and poisonous species, with over 400 members worldwide and possibly as many disputed or newly discovered species. It includes the common (“button”) mushroom, *A. bisporus*, and the field mushroom, *A. campestris*, the dominant cultivated mushrooms of the West. For many years the genus was known as *Psalliota*, a name still seen in older books. A classification of 42 species in five sections, based on tissue reactions to air and chemical reagents, was shown by restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis to need revision. As of 2018 the genus is divided into six subgenera and more than 20 sections.
